lessons.title: Your first hockey question
lessons.objective: Start a conversation about hockey with someone new to the sport.

payload.title: Your first hockey question
payload.setting: Starting a conversation with someone new to hockey.

exchanges.theirMessage: I have no idea about hockey. Where do I even start?

replies.text: What got you interested in learning about it?
replies.theirResponse: My boyfriend loves it and I want to understand.
replies.coachNote: Shows you care about her motivation.

replies.text: It's really complicated, sorry.
replies.coachNote: Discouraging from the start.

replies.text: Do you have a favorite team yet?
replies.theirResponse: I'm not sure. His is the Bruins.
replies.coachNote: Good question but assume she picks her own team.

exchanges.theirMessage: I just want to follow along when we watch games together.

replies.text: That's perfect. We can start with the basics: three 20-minute periods.
replies.theirResponse: Oh, that's way shorter than I thought!
replies.coachNote: Meet her where she is with the basics.

replies.text: Start by watching a lot of games.
replies.coachNote: Too vague; no structure.

replies.text: There's so much to learn, you'll need years.
replies.coachNote: Don't overwhelm; everyone starts somewhere.

payload.closingNote: Start with genuine curiosity about why she's interested, then build from the basics.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I don't know anything about hockey. Is it too late to start?

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: Not at all. A lot of people learned as adults. I can help you.
Hockey is pretty hard. You might not get it.
You could watch some games and figure it out on your own.

payload.translation: Reassure her and offer support. Learning hockey as an adult is totally normal.

followUps.why: Personalizes the learning to her interests.

followUps.line: Want me to explain the basics?

payload.prompt: When starting a conversation about hockey with a beginner, what is the best first step?

options.text: Ask why she is interested in learning about hockey.
Immediately explain all the rules.
Test her on hockey knowledge.

explanation.correct: Right. Understanding her motivation helps you teach in a way that matters to her.
explanation.incorrect: Start with curiosity about why she cares. That motivation shapes how you explain things.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask her why she wants to learn. That's where the real conversation starts.

payload.prompt: Saying 'hockey is complicated' to a beginner is a good way to encourage her. True or false?

explanation.correct: False. Telling someone something is complicated before they start discourages them.
explanation.incorrect: Avoid negativity when someone is interested in learning. Build confidence, not doubt.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lead with enthusiasm, not warnings. If she is curious, support that.

payload.prompt: Match the conversation starter to what makes it work.

pairs.definition: Shows you care about her motivation and helps tailor your explanation.

pairs.term: Start with basic facts: three periods, 20 minutes each.
pairs.definition: Gives her a simple foundation instead of overwhelming complexity.

pairs.term: Admit what you don't know but want to learn together.
pairs.definition: Builds confidence. You don't need to be an expert to talk about hockey.

explanation.summary: Starting a hockey conversation is about showing interest in her, not proving expertise.
explanation.sayThisLine: The best first question is about her. Everything else flows from there.

lessons.title: After a win
lessons.objective: Celebrate a win with genuine engagement and smart questions.

payload.title: After a win
payload.setting: She texts excitement right after a victory.

replies.text: Five to three! Who scored the go-ahead goal?
replies.theirResponse: Our top line got two each. Absolutely dominant.
replies.coachNote: Asking about the key goals keeps it going.

replies.text: Awesome! So happy for you!
replies.coachNote: Warm but doesn't add to the conversation.

replies.text: Cool, I guess that means they're good now.
replies.theirResponse: One win doesn't define a season, but it felt good.
replies.coachNote: Downplay her excitement and she'll pull back.

exchanges.theirMessage: The goalie was unreal tonight too.

replies.text: How many shots did he face? Sounds like he was tested.
replies.coachNote: Asking about shot volume shows you know what matters.

replies.text: That's great.
replies.coachNote: Flat agreement.

replies.text: Well, the defense helped him a lot I bet.
replies.theirResponse: They did, but he made the hard ones.
replies.coachNote: Don't dismiss the goalie; credit both.

payload.closingNote: Celebrate with her and ask about the key moments and the players who made them.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We beat our biggest rival! I'm so pumped!

payload.question: What's a good follow-up question?

options.text: How did it feel to beat them? What was the key to winning?
Great win, but you'll probably lose to them next time.
Does this guarantee you make the playoffs?

payload.translation: A good follow-up honors her excitement and asks about the game itself, not the season implications.

followUps.line: Was it close the whole game or did you dominate?
followUps.why: Explores the actual flow of the game.

followUps.line: Do they play you again this season?
followUps.why: Shows interest in the rivalry arc.

payload.prompt: After a win, what is the most useful question you can ask about the scoring?

options.text: Who scored the most goals?
Who scored the go-ahead or game-winning goal?
Did they score more than last game?

explanation.correct: Right. The go-ahead and game-winner are the moments that matter most in a win.
explanation.incorrect: The turning points in a game—the go-ahead goal, the game-winner—are what she'll remember and want to talk about.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about the key goals: the go-ahead, the game-winner. Those are the stories.

payload.prompt: After a win, downplaying the victory is a good strategy. True or false?

explanation.correct: False. Celebrate with her. Downplaying closes the conversation.
explanation.incorrect: When she is excited about a win, match her energy. Don't minimize it.
explanation.sayThisLine: She won! Celebrate that moment with her before looking ahead.

lessons.title: After a loss
lessons.objective: React to a loss with empathy and thoughtful questions.

payload.title: After a loss
payload.setting: She texts in disappointment after a tough loss.

exchanges.theirMessage: We lost 3-2. I can't believe it.

replies.text: That's a tough one, especially one-goal. What was the turning point?
replies.theirResponse: Third period they just outplayed us.
replies.coachNote: Empathy first, then a real question.

replies.text: Better luck next time.
replies.coachNote: Kind but stops the conversation.

replies.text: At least you tried. Some teams don't even show up.
replies.coachNote: Minimize her disappointment and she'll close off.

exchanges.theirMessage: I just don't understand how we let them back in.

replies.text: Sometimes teams find their rhythm in one period. Did they get a lucky goal or outwork you?
replies.coachNote: Curiosity without blame.

replies.text: It's okay, you'll get them next time.
replies.coachNote: Optimistic but she's not there yet.

replies.text: Your team isn't that good then.
replies.coachNote: Never dump on her team when she's hurting.

payload.closingNote: After a loss, empathy matters more than fixes. Ask what happened, not why she should feel better.

payload.prompt: When someone is upset about a loss, what should you do first?

options.text: Remind them of wins earlier in the season.
Show empathy and listen to what she is feeling.
Try to cheer her up with jokes.

explanation.correct: Right. Empathy first. Then she'll be ready to talk about the game itself.
explanation.incorrect: Validation comes before analysis. Let her feel the disappointment, then ask genuine questions.
explanation.sayThisLine: She's hurt about the loss. Sit with that before you try to make it better.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: I've never been so mad at a team. They played awful in the third.

payload.question: What's a good response?

options.text: They looked like they ran out of gas. Did they play back-to-back nights?
Yeah, they're just not good.
At least you're not the fan of a worse team.

payload.translation: Ask about context (schedule, injuries, situation) that might explain the collapse. Show you're thinking about why it happened.

followUps.line: Were they tired from the previous game?
Do they usually struggle in the third?

payload.prompt: Match the response to a loss with what makes it work or fail.

pairs.definition: Validates her feelings without trying to fix them immediately.

pairs.term: What happened in the third period?
pairs.definition: Asks a real question that keeps the conversation going.

pairs.term: At least other teams lose worse.
pairs.definition: Backfires. It minimizes her disappointment instead of honoring it.

explanation.summary: After a loss, lead with empathy. Questions come after she feels heard.
explanation.sayThisLine: Empathy first, curiosity second. That's the order.

lessons.title: When the ref ruins the night
lessons.objective: Talk about a controversial call without dismissing her frustration.

payload.title: When the ref ruins the night
payload.setting: She vents about a call she thinks was wrong.

exchanges.theirMessage: That penalty call was GARBAGE. He barely touched him!

replies.text: What was the call? Did it change the game?
replies.theirResponse: Tripping in the third. They scored on the power play.
replies.coachNote: Ask for details; show you're tracking with her.

replies.text: Refs are always bad.
replies.coachNote: Agreeing feels good but isn't curious.

replies.text: Refs do their best, the job is hard.
replies.coachNote: Defend refs when she's angry and she'll think you don't get it.

exchanges.theirMessage: Now we're down a goal with ten minutes left.

replies.text: Ten minutes is plenty. Your team has comebacks in them?
replies.theirResponse: Usually, but that call killed the momentum.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledge the anger but point forward.

replies.text: That's rough.
replies.coachNote: Sympathetic but passive.

replies.text: Just forget about the call and play better.
replies.coachNote: Platitudes don't help; validation does.

payload.closingNote: A bad call stings. Validate her first, then ask what happens next in the game.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Our goal got waved off for goalie interference! That was BS!

payload.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Goalie interference is the most argued call in hockey. What did you see happen?
Yeah, the ref made a bad call.
Don't worry, refs get most calls right.

payload.translation: Acknowledge that goalie interference is legitimately controversial. Ask what she saw; her view matters.

followUps.line: Was he in the crease or just nearby?

payload.prompt: When she is angry about a penalty call, defending the referee is a good idea. True or false?

explanation.correct: False. She is upset. Defending the ref makes her think you are not on her side.
explanation.incorrect: In the moment of frustration, validate her anger first. Defending refs comes later, if at all.
explanation.sayThisLine: When she is mad about a call, side with her emotion first. The ref debate can wait.

payload.prompt: What makes goalie interference the most argued call in hockey?

options.text: Everyone agrees on what it is and refs never make mistakes.
There is a gray area between contact and interference; fans see it differently than refs.
It never affects the outcome of games.

explanation.correct: Right. The rule has subjective parts, so good-faith disagreements happen all the time.
explanation.incorrect: Goalie interference is controversial because the crease rule has gray areas. Fans and officials disagree reasonably.
explanation.sayThisLine: Even refs and analysts argue about goalie interference. It's the most debated rule for a reason.

lessons.title: The goalie stole it
lessons.objective: Talk about a dominant goalie performance with the right stats.

payload.title: The goalie stole it
payload.setting: She's raving about a goalie's performance.

exchanges.theirMessage: Our goalie was absolutely standing on his head tonight. Incredible.

replies.text: How many shots did he face? And what was his save percentage looking like?
replies.coachNote: You know the numbers behind a great game.

replies.text: That's awesome!
replies.coachNote: Warm, but generic.

replies.text: So the defense was bad then.
replies.theirResponse: Actually they were solid. He just made impossible saves.
replies.coachNote: Don't assume bad defense; the goalie can just be great.

exchanges.theirMessage: If we'd lost after that performance, I would have cried.

replies.text: Did you win? Please tell me you got him the goal support he deserved.
replies.coachNote: You understand goal support matters for a goalie.

replies.text: That would be sad.
replies.coachNote: Agrees but no real engagement.

replies.text: But if he played that well why did you almost lose?
replies.theirResponse: Sometimes one great performance isn't enough.
replies.coachNote: Don't question the connection between great goaltending and results.

payload.closingNote: A goalie who stands on his head deserves goal support. Recognize both the saves and the outcome.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The goalie was the only reason we stayed in the game.

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: That's when great goaltending shows up. Did the rest of the team finally help him out?
So the team was bad?
Good thing you won then.

payload.translation: Celebrate the goalie and then ask if the team found ways to support him. Show you know goals matter.

followUps.line: How many shots did they have to defend against?
Did the team score late to give him goal support?
followUps.why: Explores whether the team stepped up.

payload.prompt: What does a .950 save percentage mean?

options.text: The goalie stopped 95 percent of the shots he faced.
The goalie played 95 percent of the game.
The goalie made 95 saves.

explanation.correct: Right. A .950 save percentage means he stopped 95 out of every 100 shots. That's excellent.
explanation.incorrect: Save percentage is saves divided by shots. .950 means 95 out of 100 shots were stopped.
explanation.sayThisLine: A .950 save percentage is elite. That's stopping almost everything.

payload.prompt: A goalie who faces 40+ shots and wins the game is mostly responsible for the win. True or false?

explanation.correct: True. 40+ shots means his team was under heavy pressure. The goalie's saves kept them in it.
explanation.incorrect: When a goalie faces 40+ shots and his team wins, the goalie's performance is the difference.
explanation.sayThisLine: Forty shots against and a win? The goalie was the star of that game.

lessons.title: Playoff nerves
lessons.objective: Talk about playoff intensity and matchup strategy.

payload.title: Playoff nerves
payload.setting: She's anxious before a playoff series starts.

exchanges.theirMessage: The playoffs start tomorrow and I'm so nervous. We're up against the defending champs.

replies.text: Defending champs are tough but they're beatable. How do your teams matchup?
replies.theirResponse: Honestly? Their top line is scary. We need our defense to match up.
replies.coachNote: Shows you understand matchups in the playoffs.

replies.text: Don't worry, you'll be fine.
replies.coachNote: Optimistic but dismisses her anxiety.

replies.text: The defending champs never win it again anyway.
replies.theirResponse: So you're saying we should lose to them?
replies.coachNote: That logic doesn't help her confidence.

exchanges.theirMessage: It's a best-of-seven so one loss doesn't end it, but still.

replies.text: True. Best-of-seven means you need four wins. If you win game one at home that helps a lot.
replies.theirResponse: That's true. First game is huge.
replies.coachNote: You understand the format strategy.

replies.text: That's good.
replies.coachNote: Flat.

replies.text: So basically it's just like the regular season then.
replies.theirResponse: No, it's totally different. It matters so much more.
replies.coachNote: Playoffs are qualitatively different; don't minimize them.

payload.closingNote: Playoff intensity is real. Validate her nerves and focus on the series structure and matchups.

payload.prompt: What does 'best-of-seven' mean in the playoffs?

options.text: The first team to win four games wins the series.
Both teams play seven games no matter what.
The team with the best regular season record wins.

explanation.correct: Right. First to four wins takes the series. It can end in 4, 5, 6 or 7 games.
explanation.incorrect: Best-of-seven means the first team to win four games wins the series. The series ends when someone gets four wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: Best-of-seven: first to four wins. It can be over in four games or go the distance.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We lost game one. Is the series over?

payload.question: What would you say?

options.text: No, it's a best-of-seven. You have time. One loss does not end it.
Yeah, pretty much. Nobody comes back from 1-0.
You could still win in seven.

payload.translation: Reassure her that one loss in a best-of-seven is not decisive. Perspective and hope matter.

followUps.line: How did you lose? Was it close?
followUps.why: Explores whether the team was competitive.

followUps.line: What does your team need to do differently in game two?

payload.prompt: Match the playoff term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The team with the better record hosts more games and plays the final game at home if needed.
Winner-take-all, a deciding game when a series is tied 3-3.
When the lower seed or worse team beats the favorite.

explanation.summary: Playoff hockey has strategic terms that shape how series play out.
explanation.sayThisLine: Home ice matters in the playoffs. Playing the last game at home is huge.

lessons.title: Watching a game together
lessons.objective: Explain the game live without condescension while she asks questions.

payload.title: Watching a game together
payload.setting: You're both watching a live game.

exchanges.theirMessage: Okay, so we're down a goal and they're pulling the goalie. What does that mean?

replies.text: They're trading the goalie for an extra skater to try to score. If they score, great. If the other team gets it in the empty net, it's a goal.
replies.theirResponse: So it's a gamble. I get it!
replies.coachNote: You explained it clearly without condescension.

replies.text: It means they want more offense.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, but who plays goalie then?
replies.coachNote: You left out the main consequence.

replies.text: You don't know? It's so simple.
replies.coachNote: Never make her feel bad for asking.

exchanges.theirMessage: Wait, they just scored with an empty net against them!

replies.text: That's the risk! They scored into the empty net. That usually ends it.
replies.theirResponse: So the pulled goalie thing backfired.
replies.coachNote: You connect the strategy to the result.

replies.text: Yeah, they scored.
replies.coachNote: She's asking for analysis, not recaps.

replies.text: That's why I would never pull the goalie.
replies.coachNote: Context matters; acknowledge both outcomes exist.

payload.closingNote: She's asking live questions to understand. Explain the logic and connect it to what's happening.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Why did they just blow the whistle? Nothing happened.

payload.question: How would you respond?

options.text: Something did happen—the ref saw something or a rule was broken. What did you see just before the whistle?
I don't know, refs are weird.
You'll learn what it means over time.

payload.translation: Invite her to notice details by asking what she saw. Teach by curiosity, not explanation.

followUps.line: Did the puck go over the glass?

payload.prompt: When watching a game together, you should explain everything before she asks. True or false?

explanation.correct: False. Let her ask. That way she learns what she wants to know, not what you think she should know.
explanation.incorrect: When watching together, respond to her questions. She'll learn faster and enjoy it more if she drives the curiosity.
explanation.sayThisLine: Don't narrate everything. Wait for her questions. She'll learn more that way.

payload.prompt: When she asks what a rule means during a game, what is the best approach?

options.text: Explain the rule in detail, including all exceptions.
Give a short explanation and keep watching the game.
Tell her you'll explain later when the game is over.

explanation.correct: Right. Keep it brief so she understands the play, then get back to the action.
explanation.incorrect: A quick explanation keeps the flow. Save the deep dive for halftime or after.
explanation.sayThisLine: Answer her question quick, then focus on the game. Depth can come later.

lessons.title: Ask about her hockey story
lessons.objective: Ask meaningful questions about her personal connection to hockey.

payload.title: Ask about her hockey story
payload.setting: A chance to ask her something deeper about her hockey fandom.

exchanges.theirMessage: I've been watching since I was seven when my dad took me to a game.

replies.text: What was that first game like? Do you remember who played?
replies.theirResponse: It was magical. I remember the sound of the crowd and the smell of the popcorn.
replies.coachNote: Shows you care about her memory, not just facts.

replies.text: That's cool. So your whole family watches?
replies.theirResponse: Just us. My mom never got into it.
replies.coachNote: Good question but not what she was sharing.

replies.text: That's a lot of years then, you must know everything.
replies.theirResponse: I know a lot, but there's always more to learn.
replies.coachNote: Don't assume; every fan still discovers new things.

exchanges.theirMessage: We've been to the home team's arena dozens of times since.

replies.text: What's your favorite memory from those games? Did you see a famous player or a big moment?
replies.theirResponse: We were there when they won the Cup in 2019. I cried.
replies.coachNote: You're honoring what this really means to her.

replies.text: That's great bonding time.
replies.coachNote: Nice, but surface-level.

replies.text: So you're basically an expert then.
replies.theirResponse: I know the team well, but hockey in general is deep.
replies.coachNote: Expertise about one team doesn't mean everything.

payload.closingNote: Her story is personal. Ask about the moments, the people, the feelings. That's where the real connection is.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: My favorite player got traded and I'm still not over it.

payload.question: How would you follow up?

options.text: How long were they your favorite? What made them special to you?
There are plenty of other players on the team.
At least they went to a good team.

payload.translation: Honor the loss. Ask about the connection, not why she should move on.

followUps.line: Did you get to see them play a lot?
followUps.why: Explores how much she followed them.

followUps.line: Do you follow them at their new team now?
followUps.why: Shows you understand the relationship extends beyond one team.

payload.prompt: What is the best question to ask someone about their hockey fandom?

options.text: How much do you know about hockey?
What's your favorite hockey memory?
Do you follow the standings?

explanation.correct: Right. A memory question opens the door to her personal story, not just facts.
explanation.incorrect: Ask about memories, not knowledge. That leads to real conversation about what hockey means to her.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about memories and feelings. That's where the real hockey love lives.

payload.prompt: Match the question type to what it reveals.

pairs.definition: Opens up her personal story and the emotions tied to hockey.

pairs.term: How many goals did your team score this season?
pairs.definition: Gets facts but misses why hockey matters to her.

pairs.term: Who taught you about hockey? Was it someone special?
pairs.definition: Explores the relationships and people tied to her fandom.

explanation.summary: The best questions connect to her personal story, not just hockey facts.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ask about the people, the moments, the feelings. That's what makes her a fan.
